transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Um… yeah. I’m here because I’ve been having this thing happen after work, after my cashier shifts, where I’ll stop and buy a ridiculous amount of takeout. Like not just a meal, but… burgers, fries, chicken, desserts, the kind of order that looks like it’s for a whole family or a bunch of people watching a game or something.

And then I’ll sit there—usually before I even go home—and I’ll eat almost all of it myself. It feels embarrassing even saying it, because I know how it sounds, but it’s been happening enough that I’m starting to feel like I can’t just pretend it’s normal or that I’m just “really hungry after work.” It’s a lot of food, and I keep doing it.
After you eat that large amount of food, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself sick, using laxatives, exercising a lot more than usual, or anything like that?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, because I don’t really think of it in, like, a plan afterward. Like I don’t sit there with some organized idea of “now I have to undo this” or anything. Mostly I just feel really ashamed and kind of grossed out with myself, and then I try not to think about it.

When you say compensate, I know you gave examples, but I guess I’m not sure what all would count. I don’t want to say the wrong thing. It’s more like afterward I just feel bad and tell myself I shouldn’t let it happen again.
When you're eating all that food at once, do you ever feel like you can't stop eating or control what or how much you're eating?

Yeah… yeah, that’s actually the part that scares me the most, I think. Because it’s not like I sit down and calmly decide, “I’m going to eat all of this.” It starts with, like, just one bite, or telling myself I’ll only have some of it and save the rest, but once I take that first bite it’s like something in me just… clicks off.

And I’ll be thinking it while it’s happening, like, “Demetrius, stop. You don’t need any more. You’re not even enjoying it anymore,” but my hands just keep going to the next thing. I’ll finish one container and then open the next one almost automatically. It’s like my brain is saying one thing and my body is doing another, and I feel like I’m watching myself do it but I can’t really interrupt it.

I know that probably sounds dramatic, but in the moment it really does feel like I don’t have control over what I’m choosing or how much is going in. I’ll keep reaching for more even when part of me is begging myself to stop.
Can you describe how long one of these eating episodes typically lasts, from the time you start eating until it’s over?

I honestly don’t know exactly. I haven’t really timed it, and when it’s happening I’m not looking at the clock in a normal way, if that makes sense. It kind of feels like the time gets blurry.

Like, I’ll start eating and I’ll be aware at first—like, “Okay, I’m eating now, I should slow down”—but then after that it’s more like I come back to myself when a lot of the food is already gone. So I could guess, but I don’t really trust my guess, because in my head it feels both really fast and also like it takes up this whole chunk of the evening.

I know it starts once I’ve got the food in front of me, and it’s over when I either run out of food or I finally just stop, but I haven’t been keeping track of how long that is. I guess I’ve been avoiding paying that much attention to it, because then it feels more real.
During these episodes, do you feel like you’re not in control of your eating, like you can’t stop even if you want to?

Yeah. I mean… yes, definitely. That’s the part I keep trying to explain, because it’s not just that I eat too much and then regret it. It feels different from just making a bad choice.

Once I take that first bite, it’s like something in me clicks off. I can be sitting there literally telling myself in my head, “Demetrius, stop. You don’t need any more. Put it down.” And I mean really saying it to myself, not after the fact, but while it’s happening. But my hands just keep reaching for the next thing anyway, like I’m on autopilot.

And it’s frustrating because I know I want to stop. I’m aware enough to know I don’t want to keep going, but I still keep going. It’s like the wanting to stop doesn’t actually do anything in that moment.
Has this eating behavior been causing you a lot of distress, or has it affected your daily life, like your work, relationships, or how you see yourself?

Yeah… it has. I mean, I still go to work. I don’t want to make it sound like I’ve completely stopped functioning, because I haven’t. I show up for my cashier shifts, I stand there, I scan people’s groceries, I do what I’m supposed to do. From the outside I probably look mostly normal.

But it’s affecting things at home a lot. The money part is a big one. I’ll spend money on food that we really don’t have to spare, and then I have to kind of… hide it or explain around it. And I hate saying that, because my wife and I are supposed to be honest with each other, but I find myself keeping secrets. Receipts, bags, charges, what I bought, what I ate. It makes me feel like I’m sneaking around in my own marriage.

And then even when she doesn’t know the exact details, I think she can feel something is off. I’m tense, I’m guilty, I’m trying to act normal, and that just makes the house feel uncomfortable. Like there’s this dishonest feeling sitting between us, even if we’re not directly talking about it.

So yeah, it’s distressing. It makes me feel ashamed of myself, and it’s starting to make home feel like a place where I’m hiding instead of just being there with my wife.
How often do these episodes happen? Like, how many times a week or month would you say this loss-of-control eating occurs?

Lately it’s been… a lot. More than I want to admit, honestly. For the last several months, I’d say it’s been happening three or four nights most weeks. Not every single night, but enough that it feels like it’s become part of the week, if that makes sense—like I’m almost waiting to see which nights it’s going to happen.

And since the foreclosure calls started, I honestly can’t remember a week where it didn’t happen at least once. I keep trying to think of a week where I got through the whole thing without one of those nights, and I can’t really come up with one. Some weeks are “better,” I guess, where it’s only once, but most weeks it’s more like three or four times. It’s embarrassing to say out loud, because when I hear myself say it, it sounds like… constant. But that’s probably the honest answer.
During these eating episodes, do you find yourself eating much more rapidly than normal?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that, honestly. I mean… I don’t sit there timing myself or anything, so I don’t know if it’s “much more rapidly” in a way someone else would notice.

It feels like I’m not really paying attention to the pace, if that makes sense. Sometimes I look down and realize more food is gone than I expected, but I don’t know if that means I was eating fast or just not really thinking while I was doing it. I guess I haven’t specifically noticed, like, “Oh, I’m chewing really fast” or “I’m rushing.” It’s more that the whole thing kind of blurs together.

So… maybe? But I don’t want to say yes if I’m not sure. I just know I’m not eating in a normal, relaxed way during those times.
Do you usually eat alone during these episodes because you’re embarrassed about how much you’re eating?

Yeah… usually, yes. That’s probably one of the parts I feel the most embarrassed about.

I don’t really want anyone to see it, especially my wife. It’s not like I want to sit at the table and have her watch me eat that much, because then I’d have to see her seeing me, if that makes sense. So I find ways to do it where I’m by myself. Sometimes I’ll eat in the car, like in a parking lot, before I even come home. I’ll just sit there with the bags next to me and eat it there because it feels safer than bringing it inside and having to explain it.

Other times I’ll wait until my wife is asleep. I’ll kind of listen for the house to get quiet, and then I’ll go eat. And afterward I’m really careful about the evidence, which sounds awful to say. I’ll stuff the bags and wrappers and receipts down into the trash so she won’t see how much I had, or so it doesn’t look obvious right on top.

It’s definitely because I’m ashamed. If I wasn’t embarrassed, I don’t think I’d be hiding it like that.
During these eating episodes, do you find yourself eating until you feel uncomfortably full, even when you know you’ve had enough?

Yeah… that happens a lot. More than I want to admit.

It’s like I’ll know I’ve had enough—sometimes I know it pretty early, honestly—but I don’t stop there. I keep going past that point where it’s just “full,” and then it turns into this really uncomfortable feeling, like my stomach gets tight and stretched out. There have been a lot of nights where it actually hurts, not just feeling stuffed, but painful enough that I have to kind of lean the seat back in the car and just sit there for a while because sitting upright feels awful.

Or if I’m at home, I’ll lie still in bed and try not to move much, just waiting for it to pass. I’ll be thinking, “Why did I keep going? I knew I was already done,” but by then I’ve already eaten way past where I should’ve stopped. It’s embarrassing because it’s not like I don’t realize it’s happening. I do realize it, at least partway through, but I still keep eating until my body feels miserable.

Can you tell me if, during these episodes, you feel like you’re eating an unusually large amount of food within a short period of time—like within a couple of hours—compared to what most people would eat in that same time frame?

Yeah… yes. I mean, that’s honestly one of the main reasons I’m here, because it’s not like I’m just having an extra meal or snacking too much.

After my shifts at the register, especially if I’m already stressed or just kind of worn out, I’ll stop and buy takeout, but the amount is… it’s huge. Like, I’m not talking about one burger and fries. I’ll get enough that it would look like I’m bringing food home for a whole family—multiple burgers, large fries, chicken, desserts, drinks, that kind of thing. Sometimes I feel like the cashier must assume I’m ordering for several people, and I kind of let them think that because it feels less humiliating.

And then I’ll sit there and eat almost all of it by myself before I go home. Usually in the car, and it’s all within a pretty short stretch of time. Not like I’m grazing over the whole day. It’s more like I buy this massive order and then it’s just… gone. And afterward I look at the wrappers and it’s really hard to believe one person ate that much, but I did.

So compared to what most people would eat in a couple hours? Yeah. Definitely unusually large.

There have been a lot of nights where it actually hurts, not just feeling stuffed, but painful enough that I have to kind of lean the seat back in the car and just sit there for a while because sitting upright feels awful.

Or if I’m at home, I’ll lie still in bed and try not to move much, just waiting for it to pass. I’ll be thinking, “Why did I keep going? I knew I was already done,” but by then I’ve already eaten way past where I should’ve stopped. It’s embarrassing because it’s not like I don’t realize it’s happening. I do realize it, at least partway through, but I still keep eating until my body feels miserable.

These features are consistent with binge eating disorder (F50.2). No features suggesting anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, or other specified feeding or eating disorders (e.g., purging, restrictive eating, etc.) were endorsed, maintaining F50.2 and F50.9 as the most relevant differentials. No new exclusion criteria identified.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences eating large amounts of food in a discrete period of time, which is a key feature distinguishing binge eating episodes from other eating behaviors.
doctor.question: Can you tell me if, during these episodes, you feel like you’re eating an unusually large amount of food within a short period of time—like within a couple of hours—compared to what most people would eat in that same time frame?

target_item.name: Eating_Large_Amount
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because after my cashier shifts I keep buying these huge takeout orders—like enough burgers, fries, chicken, and desserts for a family—and I’ll sit there and eat almost all of it myself before I go home.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether the episodes involve eating an unusually large amount of food within a discrete period of time compared with what most people would eat.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes. I mean, that’s honestly one of the main reasons I’m here, because it’s not like I’m just having an extra meal or snacking too much.

After my shifts at the register, especially if I’m already stressed or just kind of worn out, I’ll stop and buy takeout, but the amount is… it’s huge. Like, I’m not talking about one burger and fries. I’ll get enough that it would look like I’m bringing food home for a whole family—multiple burgers, large fries, chicken, desserts, drinks, that kind of thing. Sometimes I feel like the cashier must assume I’m ordering for several people, and I kind of let them think that because it feels less humiliating.

And then I’ll sit there and eat almost all of it by myself before I go home. Usually in the car, and it’s all within a pretty short stretch of time. Not like I’m grazing over the whole day. It’s more like I buy this massive order and then it’s just… gone. And afterward I look at the wrappers and it’s really hard to believe one person ate that much, but I did.

So compared to what most people would eat in a couple hours? Yeah. Definitely unusually large.

inference.note: The patient's symptoms align with binge eating disorder (F50.2), including loss of control during eating episodes, consuming large amounts of food in a discrete period, eating until uncomfortably full, eating alone due to embarrassment, and experiencing distress and interpersonal consequences. There is insufficient evidence to support F50.9 (eating disorder unspecified) as the presentation is specific and meets full criteria for binge eating disorder.
